newsitem.title: USA: Dallas Cowboys try to clean up their act.
newsitem.headline: Dallas Cowboys try to clean up their act.

text.p: Battered by a string of sex and drugs scandals, the Dallas Cowboys football team has launched a multimillion-dollar programme to teach some of its wayward players how to behave properly off the field.

Team owner Jerry Jones told The Dallas Morning News on Thursday that he is setting up a special department devoted to improving player behaviour with four managers and 10 staff members as well as an advisory board of former players.
"It's a get-smart policy," Jones told the newspaper. "The fans of the Cowboys deserve this type of intense commitment to good behaviour."

A long list of scandals involving drug abuse and players cavorting with topless dancers and prostitutes has alienated many Cowboys fans and hurt the reputation of an organisation once known as "America's Team."

Star wide receiver Michael Irvin last year was put on four years probation when he pleaded no contest to drug possession charges after being caught in a motel room with cocaine, marijuana and two topless dancers.
The Cowboys also had five players suspended by the National Football League for alcohol or drugs abuse over a 14-month period ending last November.
The team's new department in charge of improving that record will hire special managers for security, player development and assistance, psychology and spirituality.
Jones stopped short of saying that any player who gets caught up in another scandal would be fired but suggested non-compliance would bring repercussions.
"If we see people that can't recognise the value of this, that'll impact my decision on whether they stay on the football team or not," Jones told the Morning News.
The Cowboys' plan has been devised by Calvin Hill, who played for the team from 1969 to 1974 and is the father of the well-behaved NBA superstar Grant Hill.
Troy Aikman, the Cowboys' star quarterback who maintained a spotless reputation even as some of his teammates strayed, welcomed the new plan. "I think this can help," Aikman told the Morning News.
